name: Tanning gummies / supplements
lead: Tanning gummies and tanning pills are oral products sold to give skin a deeper, tan-looking colour without sun or sunbeds. They usually rely on carotenoid pigments, most often beta-carotene, and in older products canthaxanthin, which are absorbed and stored in the body so that the skin takes on a golden-orange tint.[1][2] People use them as a swallowed alternative to sunless tanning lotions, aiming for an even, all-over colour that does not depend on UV exposure.

Carotenoids are the pigments that colour carrots, tomatoes and some fish. Taken in large amounts over time, they can change skin colour; the tint is described as long-lasting and can take months to fade after intake stops.[1] Canthaxanthin deposits throughout the body including the fat layer under the skin, producing an orange-brown shade.[1][2] Because the colour comes from the pigment itself, it does not involve melanin or sun exposure.

In the United States, the FDA has stated that no tanning pills are approved and has treated products containing canthaxanthin as adulterated cosmetics, issuing warning letters to marketers, including one dated 5 April 2005.[2] The American Cancer Society notes that the FDA has approved some of these colour additives for foods but not as tanning agents.[1] No published clinical trial has tested a modern tanning gummy for cosmetic outcomes.

chain: Swallow a carotenoid pigment (beta-carotene or canthaxanthin)
Pigment is stored in skin and the fat layer beneath it
Skin takes on a golden-orange, tan-like colour
angle.text: The colour change comes from the pigment accumulating in the body, so the skin can look warmer and more bronzed without UV exposure. The shade is typically golden-orange rather than the brown produced by melanin, and it builds up over weeks of regular intake and fades slowly.

paras: Oral tanners are marketed as chews, gummies, tablets or capsules. Their active ingredients are carotenoids: beta-carotene, which the body also converts to vitamin A, and canthaxanthin, a keto-carotenoid pigment used as a food and feed colourant.[1][2] Lycopene, another carotenoid, is described in encyclopedic sources as a food colourant but without discussion of tanning use.[1]
Excess carotene in the blood and skin produces a harmless yellow-orange tint known as carotenaemia or carotenoderma, which is the mechanism these products rely on.[1]

Canthaxanthin pills were sold to simulate a tan, with the pigment depositing in the subcutaneous fat and giving the skin a golden-orange hue.[2] Tanning doses are much larger than the amounts used to colour foods.[1]

In the late 1980s, reversible crystal-like deposits in the retina were reported in a limited number of people who had taken very high amounts from tanning pills; they disappeared after stopping and the affected people recovered.[2] The FDA also links such pills to canthaxanthin retinopathy, liver injury and hives, citing the American Academy of Dermatology.[2] A 2011 study by Hueber and colleagues reported reversible retinal deposits and no lasting structural changes.[2]

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives set an acceptable daily intake for canthaxanthin as a food colour of 0.03 mg per kg of body weight in 1995; the EU Scientific Committee for Food accepted it in 1997 and EFSA reconfirmed it in 2010.[2] These figures concern use as a food additive, not tanning.

The American Cancer Society states that beta-carotene is not FDA-approved as a tanning agent and that such additives may be harmful at the high levels used in tanning pills.[1] High-dose synthetic beta-carotene supplements have been linked to a higher lung cancer rate in smokers.[1]

Oral tanners are discussed in appearance communities as one of several routes to a bronzed look alongside sunless lotions, sprays and sunbeds, with the appeal that colour is even and needs no application. Reports of orange tinting, especially on palms and in skin folds, are a common theme when carotenoid products are discussed.

timeline.event: Retinal crystal deposits reported in some people taking very high amounts of canthaxanthin from tanning pills; they resolved after stopping.[2]
JECFA sets an acceptable daily intake for canthaxanthin as a food colour.[2]
FDA warning letter (5 April) to a firm marketing a canthaxanthin product, describing such products as adulterated cosmetics.[2]
Hueber and colleagues report reversible retinal deposits without lasting structural change.[2]

card.summary: Carotenoid chews and pills sold to deepen a tan; no tanning approval and past retinal and liver concerns.
card.note: FDA has warned against tanning pills.

quick.overview:
These are chews or pills, often with carotenoids, marketed to make skin look tanner.

No tanning pill is FDA-approved, and no trial supports the gummy format.
quick.mechanism: Carotenoids such as canthaxanthin deposit in fat under the skin and tint it golden-orange.[2]
quick.risks: High-dose canthaxanthin has been linked to retinal deposits, liver injury and hives;[2] beta-carotene to lung cancer in smokers at high doses.[1]
